Yes, FDA can force a company to stop distribution or recall talc body powder if the Secretary determines there is a reasonable probability that the product is adulterated or misbranded and use of or exposure to it could cause serious adverse health consequences or death. This authority is granted under FD&C Act § 611(a), which allows the Secretary to issue an order requiring immediate cessation of distribution or recall, even if the responsible person refuses to act voluntarily [1].

The authority to require cessation of distribution or recall is established in FD&C Act § 611(a) [21 U.S.C. 364g(a)], which provides that if the Secretary determines there is a reasonable probability that a cosmetic is adulterated or misbranded and exposure could cause serious adverse health consequences or death, the Secretary may issue an order requiring immediate cessation of distribution or recall, even if the responsible person refuses to act voluntarily [1].

The responsible person must be given an opportunity for an informal hearing within 10 days after the issuance of the order to determine whether adequate evidence justifies the order, as specified in FD&C Act § 611(b) [21 U.S.C. 364g(b)] [2].

If the Secretary issues a recall or distribution cessation order, the responsible person must immediately cease distribution or recall the product and provide notification as required by the order, as mandated in FD&C Act § 611(d) [21 U.S.C. 364g(d)] [4].

The Secretary may also require the responsible person to notify appropriate persons—including manufacturers, distributors, importers, and retailers—and the public about the recall or cessation of distribution, as specified in FD&C Act § 611(e) [21 U.S.C. 364g(e)] [5].

In conducting a recall, the Secretary shall ensure that a press release is published and alerts are issued to consumers and retailers, including details such as the name of the product, description of the risk, and information about similar non-affected products, as required in FD&C Act § 611(f) [21 U.S.C. 364g(f)] [6].

The authority to issue a recall order is not delegated; it must be exercised by the Commissioner, as stated in FD&C Act § 611(g) [21 U.S.C. 364g(g)] [7].

Nothing in this section limits or affects the Secretary’s ability to request or participate in a voluntary recall, or to issue an order under any other provision of the subchapter, per FD&C Act § 611(h) [21 U.S.C. 364g(h)] [8].
